title: Check yourself: The memory file, settings layers and permission rules

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A repository holds credentials in `.env`, and Claude must never open them. One teammate writes a sentence about it in the memory file, and another adds a path block to the shared configuration. Which one actually stops it?

options.text: The `Read` rule, which is checked before each call runs
options.says: The page says "Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration", while "Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow."

options.text: The memory sentence, which Claude Code enforces once it loads
options.says: Ruled out because memory files are "context, not enforced configuration", so the sentence only asks.

options.text: Both entries equally, since each is read before any tool call
options.says: Ruled out because a memory file is loaded "at the start of every conversation" and still only asks, while a deny rule sits first in "deny, then ask, then allow".

options.text: Neither entry, since a project file never beats a user file
options.says: Ruled out because "A key set at a higher level overrides the same key set lower down" is about the same key, and since "they combine across layers", a project deny still applies.

questions.stem: A settings file allows `Bash(git log *)` and another layer lists `Bash(git *)` under deny. What happens when Claude runs `git log --oneline`?

options.text: It is allowed, because the allow rule names the narrower command here
options.says: Ruled out because "rule specificity doesn't change the order", so a narrower allow does not win.

options.text: It is allowed, because the later layer replaces the earlier one in full
options.says: Ruled out because "they combine across layers", so the later layer does not replace the earlier one.

options.text: It asks, because the two rules cancel each other out in the end
options.says: Ruled out because the first match decides and the rules never cancel: "An allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule".

options.text: It is refused, because rules of that kind are checked first and win
options.says: The page says "Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order determines the outcome, and rule specificity doesn't change the order."

questions.stem: A developer wants to use a cheaper model on their own machine without changing it for the team. Where does the setting go?

options.text: The shared project file, which is committed with the code of the team
options.says: Ruled out because "The team's choices go in the shared project file, which is committed", so the choice would reach the whole team.

options.text: The managed settings, which override every other layer of the settings
options.says: Ruled out because managed settings are for "A rule that must hold regardless of what any developer writes", and are not a personal file.

options.text: The local project file, which is kept out of version control
options.says: The page puts "A personal override" in the local file, which "belongs in `.gitignore`".

options.text: The memory file, which names the model in one plain sentence of text
options.says: Ruled out because the memory file "asks" and does not set a model: "A memory file asks and a hook enforces."
